title: Sockets, protocols, timeouts, and message framing
sources: Python 3.14 documentation: socket and selectors modules
IETF RFC 9293 TCP byte-stream semantics; reviewed 2026-10-03
masterChecklist: Sockets, HTTP concepts, REST APIs, requests, retries, idempotency, pagination, rate limits, error handling
Protocol boundaries, connection lifecycle, timeouts, partial reads/writes and message framing
Networking reliability, backpressure, observability and safe resource limits
whyItMatters: Network code does not receive a perfect complete message every time it calls receive. Connections can be slow, closed, or return partial data. A protocol must define how a receiver knows where one message ends.
simpleExplanation: A socket is an endpoint for sending bytes. TCP is a stream of bytes, not a built-in list of messages. Message framing is the rule that separates messages—for example, a length prefix or a newline in a protocol that forbids newlines in values. Timeouts limit how long a program waits so one stalled peer does not freeze all work.
mentalModel: A byte stream is a water hose, not a stack of labeled buckets. Framing is the rule for filling bottles: use a marked length or a clear divider so the receiver knows when one bottle is complete.
outcomes: Explain why one recv call may not contain a full application message.
State why every network boundary needs a timeout policy.
Distinguish transport bytes from an application protocol.

realWorldExample.scenario: A local report tool reads newline-delimited fictional events from a controlled stream abstraction.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Assuming each chunk equals one event can combine two events or split one event, causing corrupted parsing or stalled work.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Define framing, buffer incomplete data, enforce maximum message size, set read/write timeouts, validate parsed data, and record safe connection diagnostics.

explanation: chunks model arbitrary pieces of a byte/text stream without opening a real socket.
buffer keeps an incomplete message until a delimiter arrives.
split with a limit of 1 removes one complete framed line at a time.
The returned leftover shows that 'three' has not received its terminating newline and is not treated as complete.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Add a final '\n' to the last chunk and predict how the leftover changes.

procedure: Choose a protocol and write its framing, encoding, limits, and error rules.
Set explicit connect/read/write timeouts appropriate to the product.
Buffer partial input until a complete framed message exists.
Reject oversized or malformed messages before expensive work.
Close connections and log safe summary information when boundaries fail.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming recv returns one whole message.
commonMistakes.why: Stream transport can split or combine application data arbitrarily.
commonMistakes.avoid: Implement a documented framing and buffering rule.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using no timeout for remote I/O.
commonMistakes.why: A stalled peer can consume a worker indefinitely.
commonMistakes.avoid: Define bounded timeouts and a retry/failure policy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accepting unlimited input size before parsing.
commonMistakes.why: It can exhaust memory or processing resources.
commonMistakes.avoid: Set a protocol-level size limit and reject safely.

lab.title: Reassemble fictional newline-framed events
lab.safety: Uses only local string chunks; it does not open a network socket.
lab.starterCode:
def receive_lines(chunks):
    buffer = ''
    messages = []
    # Add chunks, move complete newline-ended messages to messages, retain leftover.
    return messages, buffer
guidedSteps: While a newline is present, split only once.
Append the complete line to messages.
checks: Handles a chunk containing more than one line.
lab.solutionExplanation: The function separates only completed newline-framed messages and safely preserves a partial final message for later input.
challenges: Find the bug: append buffer as a message after every chunk.
Experiment: add a maximum permitted line length and define the safe rejection behavior.
lab.testCode:
assert receive_lines(['ab', 'c\nx', 'y\nlast']) == (['abc', 'xy'], 'last')
assert receive_lines([]) == ([], '')
assert receive_lines(['\n']) == ([''], '')
print('PASS: newline message framing')

projectConnection.milestone: Write a protocol note defining framing, maximum message size, timeout policy, and invalid-message behavior before adding any real network adapter.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The importer never assumes one transport chunk equals one application message and has a documented limit for untrusted input.

assessment.question: Why is TCP not automatically a message protocol?
assessment.answer: It delivers a byte stream; an application must define how messages are separated.
assessment.explanation: A recv call can contain partial or multiple messages.

assessment.question: What does message framing do?
assessment.answer: It tells the receiver where one application message starts or ends.
assessment.explanation: Delimiters and length prefixes are common strategies.

assessment.question: Why use timeouts in network code?
assessment.answer: They prevent a stalled operation from waiting without bound.
assessment.explanation: A product must decide what to do after the time limit.
